subject: Copywriting
title: The Power of Imperatives
description: A quick win: understand The Power of Imperatives.

hook.text: 'Just Do It.' 'Think Different.' 'Eat Fresh.' 'Obey Your Thirst.' The most powerful slogans are commands.

buildup.text: Imperative slogans give the reader a role. You're not a spectator—you're an actor. The verb creates action in the mind.

discovery.text: Research shows imperative sentences are processed faster than declaratives.

twist.text: Imperatives only work when the brand has earned the authority to command. A startup can't say 'Do It' like Nike can.

climax.text: The best imperatives feel like encouragement, not orders. 'Think Different' invites; 'Buy Now' demands. Tone matters.

punchline.text: Commands drive action. But only earned authority can command.

quiz.question: Why do imperative slogans work well?
options: They give the reader a role and are processed faster

details.summary: Imperative slogans — direct commands like 'Just Do It,' 'Think Different,' and 'Obey Your Thirst' — are among the most powerful forms of persuasion. By issuing a command, the brand assumes authority and invites immediate action. The imperative voice eliminates hesitation.
details.whyItMatters: Commands create a sense of urgency and authority that descriptive slogans lack. Learning when to use the imperative voice is essential for writing slogans that drive action.
takeaways: Imperative slogans command action, creating urgency
Commands assume authority and position the brand as a leader
The imperative voice works best for aspirational or action brands

faq.question: Why are imperative slogans so common in advertising?
faq.answer: Imperatives cut through noise by demanding action rather than describing features. They compress the entire value proposition into a command: 'Just Do It' implies Nike will help you overcome hesitation. The audience becomes the subject of the sentence.

faq.question: When should a brand avoid using imperative slogans?
faq.answer: Luxury and hospitality brands often avoid commands because they feel presumptuous. A brand like Hermès would never say 'Buy This Bag.' Imperatives work for aspirational, empowerment, or performance brands but can feel aggressive for softer brand identities.
